related_questions.question: How do you know if you have a salivary stone?

text_blocks.snippet: Salivary stones, also known as sialolithiasis, are mineral deposits that form in the salivary glands and can cause pain and swelling, particularly during meals when saliva production increases. If you suspect you have a salivary stone, you might experience pain, swelling, and tenderness in your jaw, cheek, or neck, which worsens when eating. Other symptoms can include difficulty swallowing, a dry mouth, a strange taste, and a painful lump under your tongue.
snippet_highlighted_words: you might experience pain, swelling, and tenderness in your jaw, cheek, or neck, which worsens when eating

list.title: Pain and Swelling:
list.snippet: The most noticeable symptoms are pain and swelling in the area of the affected salivary gland, especially during or after eating. This pain can be intermittent or persistent.

list.title: Worsening with Eating:
list.snippet: Salivary stones often cause increased pain and swelling when you start eating or anticipating food, as this stimulates saliva production.

list.title: Lump or Swelling:
list.snippet: You might feel a lump or swelling in your jaw, cheek, or under your tongue.

list.title: Dry Mouth:
list.snippet: If a stone blocks the flow of saliva, it can lead to a dry mouth.

list.title: Difficulty Swallowing or Opening Mouth:
list.snippet: In some cases, the swelling from a stone can make it difficult to swallow or open your mouth fully.

list.title: Strange Taste:
list.snippet: Some individuals report a strange or bitter taste in their mouth due to the stone or infection.

list.title: Fever:
list.snippet: If a salivary stone leads to an infection, you might experience fever, chills, and redness.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to see a doctor or dentist if you experience any of the above symptoms, especially if they are persistent or accompanied by signs of infection (fever, redness, pus). They can properly diagnose the issue and recommend appropriate treatment.

related_questions.question: What are the symptoms of a blocked salivary gland?

text_blocks.snippet: Symptoms of a blocked salivary gland include swelling and pain in the face or neck, particularly near the affected gland (around the ear or under the jaw), which may worsen during or after eating. Other symptoms can include dry mouth, a bad or foul taste in the mouth, difficulty opening the mouth, and in some cases, fever and chills.

Other symptoms can include dry mouth, a bad or foul taste in the mouth, difficulty opening the mouth, and in some cases, fever and chills

text_blocks.snippet: A blocked salivary gland, also known as sialadenitis or salivary duct obstruction, occurs when a salivary stone or other obstruction prevents saliva from flowing properly from the gland into the mouth. This can lead to a buildup of saliva and potential infection.
Here's a more detailed breakdown of the symptoms:

list.snippet: Swelling and Pain: The most common symptom is swelling and pain in the area of the affected salivary gland. This may be a dull ache that comes and goes, or it can be more severe and persistent. The swelling is often more noticeable when eating because the gland produces more saliva in response to food.
Dry Mouth: When saliva flow is blocked, the mouth can become dry and uncomfortable.
Abnormal Taste: Some people experience a bad or foul taste in their mouth due to the stagnation of saliva.
Difficulty Opening the Mouth: In some cases, the swelling can make it difficult to fully open the mouth.
Fever and Chills: If a blocked gland becomes infected, fever and chills can develop as the body fights off the infection.
Pus Drainage: In severe cases, pus may drain into the mouth from the affected gland.

related_questions.question: How can you get rid of a salivary stone?
related_questions.snippet: Most of the time, salivary gland stones go away on their own with conservative treatment. You might be able to push the stone out of your salivary duct by drinking lots of water, applying heat or massaging the area. You can also try sucking on lemon drops or other sour candy to stimulate saliva production.

text_blocks.snippet: Salivary stones, also known as sialolithiasis, can cause pain and swelling in the salivary glands, particularly when eating. Other symptoms include dry mouth, difficulty swallowing or opening the mouth, and potentially bad breath. Infections can also develop, leading to fever and pus drainage.
